conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. I understand you were brought in after your caregiver found you with low blood sugar and some shaking movements?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I was feeling weak and then my arms started jerking. I couldn’t control it. My sugar was really low, but it came up after they gave me juice.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Low sugar can cause twitching, but since it’s still happening, we need to look into other causes. We’ve checked your labs and found your sodium is low, and you have an infection marker slightly elevated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My sodium? I didn’t know that could affect me like this. Is that why I’m twitching?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might be part of it, especially since you're on dialysis. But we also think one of your antibiotics—Ciprofloxacin—could be causing these jerks. It’s known to do that in some patients, especially with kidney issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I’ve been on that since my last hospital stay for the foot infection. Should I stop it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve already stopped it. We’re switching you to an IV antibiotic called Ceftazidime, which is safer for you and still treats the bone infection in your heel.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds better. But my leg still hurts a lot. Is the infection getting worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The infection is still there, and we’re treating it aggressively. But the teams—podiatry, vascular, and infectious disease—still believe a below-the-knee amputation is the best long-term solution to heal you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know they’ve said that before. I just need more time to think. I’m not ready for surgery yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We understand. You don’t have to decide now. But we want you to know it’s not just about infection—it’s also about your dialysis access. The transplant team says they can’t place a new graft until the infection is gone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can’t get a better dialysis line until my leg is taken care of?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It’s all connected. We’re not pushing, but we want you to have all the information when you talk to the surgeons again as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs improved overnight. Your sodium went up to 132 after your dialysis session, which is much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. And the jerking? I haven’t noticed it since last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a great sign. We think stopping the Cipro helped. We’ll keep monitoring, but it looks like the myoclonus is resolving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. I was really scared something was wrong with my brain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your neurology—your reflexes and mental status are intact. No signs of stroke or seizure. This was likely a medication and metabolic issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You just finished dialysis. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A bit tired, but okay. My leg is still sore, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve given your IV antibiotic after dialysis, as planned. The infection markers are coming down, but the wound is still concerning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the urine test? I remember they said something about bacteria.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The urine had mixed bacteria, but it looks like contamination. No active UTI, so we’re not treating it. But we still recommend straight catheterization every other day to prevent infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My nurse does that at home. I have a urology appointment coming up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, next week. They’ll help decide if you need a long-term catheter or other options.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We reviewed everything with the team. Your twitching is gone, sodium is stable, and infection signs are improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I might be able to go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely tomorrow. You’ll continue IV antibiotics during dialysis and keep taking Flagyl at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my insulin? I was on 30 units, but you changed it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We lowered it to 25 units because your sugars were running low. You can go back to 30 if they stay stable, but we’ll watch closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. And Gabapentin? I’ve been on it for years for nerve pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We paused it at first because it can rarely cause jerking, but since your symptoms improved without restarting it, we’ll let you resume at home unless you notice any issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my heart medicine? I’m not on blood thinners anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s right. We stopped warfarin due to concerns about calciphylaxis, but dermatology said it’s unlikely. With your high stroke risk, your primary team should re-evaluate restarting a blood thinner soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll ask my doctor. I don’t want to have a stroke.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—we’re discharging you today. Your labs are stable, no more twitching, and you’re feeling better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue IV antibiotics at dialysis, take Flagyl three times a day, and keep your insulin as prescribed. The visiting nurse will catheterize you every other day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the leg? When do I see the surgeons?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get a call from podiatry and vascular surgery within the week. They’ll help you decide about the amputation. We know it’s a big decision, but it’s the best chance for healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll think about it. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. Call us if your weight goes up more than three pounds, or if you have fever, pain, or confusion. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in before you leave. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’ve got it all. Thank you for helping me feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll see you in follow-up soon. Stay safe.
